Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Sanskrit tradition.

pronunciation.approximation: 'SHAKTI' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

kin.label: Root
kin.form: √śak, 'to be able, to have power' — śak-ti, the abstract noun of capacity (Monier-Williams, s.v. śakti)

kin.label: Vedic relative
kin.form: śacī-, 'might, help' — Indra's personified power and consort in the Ṛgveda (RV 10.86), the earliest ancestor of the goddess

pronunciation.note: Śakti is Tier 1: the palatal ś — the sibilant IAST writes Ś, the sound English flattens to 'sh' — is a distinctive diacritic-bearing letter that the ASCII form loses. The word itself is the abstract of √śak, 'to be able': the name of power, marked as Sanskrit by the very letter that carries its meaning.

domains.title: Power
domains.subtitle: Power, Energy, Divine Feminine
domains.lead: Śakti is power itself: the energy without which the god is a lifeless body — śiva without śakti is a corpse. She is the active power of the divine personified as the goddess: consort of Śiva in the Purāṇas, the Devī who slays the buffalo-demon in the Devīmāhātmya, and the coiled force of Kuṇḍalinī in Tantra.

cards.name: Śakti, the Active Power
cards.desc: The name means power, ability, energy — the operative might of a deity personified as his consort (Monier-Williams, s.v.).

cards.name: Devīmāhātmya
cards.desc: In the Caṇḍī (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 81–93) the gods' combined śaktis blaze forth as the Devī who destroys Mahiṣāsura.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: The palatal Ś — IAST's ś, the sound English writes 'sh' — is recovered from the ASCII flattening, letter by letter.

cards.name: Original Attestation
cards.desc: Devanagari शक्ति — attested from the Ṛgveda's śacī-, 'might', onward as śakti, 'power, ability, energy'.

symbols.name: The kuṇḍalinī serpent
symbols.meaning: Coiled at the base of the spine — the latent śakti that Tantra raises through the cakras to unite with Śiva at the crown

symbols.name: The triśūla (trident)
symbols.meaning: Śiva's weapon as energy — the three powers of will, knowledge, and action (icchā, jñāna, kriyā) personified

symbols.name: The śrīcakra
symbols.meaning: The nine-interlocked-triangle diagram of Śrīvidyā — śakti worshipped as pure geometry, the goddess as the map of her own power

symbols.name: The sword of the Devī
symbols.meaning: The blade with which Caṇḍikā beheads Mahiṣāsura — divine power as the weapon the gods only hold because she wields it

symbols.name: The lotus (padma)
symbols.meaning: The unfolding seat of the goddess — energy rising, petal by petal, toward the thousand-petalled crown

mythology.lead: Śakti is both a theological principle and a goddess with a story. The Veda knows her as śacī, the might of Indra; the Purāṇas give her a body, a husband, and a battlefield; the Tantras make her the equal — in places the superior — of the god she empowers.

myths.title: Śacī, the Might Before the Goddess
myths.text: Before Śakti had temples she had a word. The Ṛgveda uses śacī-, 'might, help, assistance,' for the power that makes Indra the conqueror of Vṛtra, and already personifies it: Indra is śacīpati, 'lord of śacī,' and his consort bears the name Śacī/Indrāṇī — celebrated in RV 10.86, where Indrāṇī boasts she is greater than all the wives of the gods. The abstract noun never quite loses its abstractness: Śakti the goddess grows directly out of śakti the grammatical fact, the capacity to act. The interpretive core of later Śākta theology is already visible in the Vedic idiom — a god's power is not his possession but his partner. What the Veda states as a linguistic intuition, that might is feminine and stands beside the god as his wife, the Purāṇas will raise into a cosmos.

myths.title: The Power of All the Gods
myths.text: The Devīmāhātmya (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 81–93) stages the supreme demonstration. When the buffalo-demon Mahiṣa overthrows the gods, they gather and pour forth their śaktis — a flame-mass of energy issues from Śiva, from Viṣṇu, from Indra, from each — and the blazes converge into female form: the ten-armed Devī, 'the śakti of all, whose form is the power of all beings.' Riding a lion, armed with every god's own weapon, she battles Mahiṣa across nine days and nights, cuts off the buffalo head, and pins the demon with her spear as he emerges in human form; the gods hymn her as the power behind their power — 'only in you do we triumph.' The text's claim is the charter of Śākta religion: the goddess is not one deity among many but the energy by which every deity acts, and without her the pantheon stands unarmed.

myths.title: The Sacrifice of Dakṣa
myths.text: The Purāṇic cycle tells how Śakti once lived with Śiva as Satī, daughter of Dakṣa. Dakṣa held a great sacrifice and invited every god but his son-in-law; when Satī came uninvited and found no portion set for her husband, she reproached her father and immolated herself in the sacrificial fire. Śiva, mad with grief, danced the world-threatening tāṇḍava with her corpse on his shoulder until Viṣṇu cut the body apart with his discus, and where each part fell a śakti-pīṭha — 'seat of śakti' — arose, fifty-one in the standard count (Devī Purāṇa; expanded in the later Devībhāgavata). The myth grounds Śākta geography: India's great goddess shrines are literally her scattered body, her yoni at Kāmākhyā above all. Its deeper teaching is the one the Tantras repeat endlessly — the god without his śakti is not merely bereaved but broken.

myths.title: Śiva Without Śakti Is a Corpse
myths.text: Tantric theology states the doctrine as a pun and means it literally: śaktiṃ vinā śivaḥ śavaḥ — 'without Śakti, Śiva is a corpse.' Abhinavagupta's Parātrīśikā-vivaraṇa and Kṣemarāja's Uddyota on the Śivasūtra teach that Śiva is pure light (prakāśa) and Śakti the self-awareness (vimarśa) by which light knows itself: consciousness without energy is inert, energy without consciousness is blind, and liberation is their union. The Śrīvidyā schools worshipped the union as the śrīcakra and the goddess Tripurasundarī; the yoga traditions mapped it as kuṇḍalinī, the coiled serpent-power raised through the cakras to meet Śiva at the crown. The sentence no myth could improve on: the corpse and the god are divided by exactly one thing — the presence of the feminine power.

myths.title: The Power of the Word
myths.text: The grammarian-philosopher Bhartṛhari (5th–7th c.) closed the circle by making śakti a theory of language: the Vākyapadīya teaches that every word carries an innate śakti, an expressive power by which it means anything at all — distinguished from the secondary powers lakṣaṇā and vyañjanā. Grammar, like the goddess, is the invisible energy that makes signification happen. The Mahābhārata had already used śakti for a god-forged weapon — the spear that Karṇa carries into his last battle is named Śakti, the power given him by Indra in exchange for his divine armor. From might to missile to meaning, the word's career traces the goddess's own: wherever something acts, the tradition first names the agent — and then, looking closer, names the energy that acts through him.

lore.syncretism: Buddhism absorbed śakti as readily as it debated it. Vajrayāna pairs every male buddha with a female consort — Prajñā as the śakti of Upāya, wisdom as the power of compassion — and elevates Tārā, Vajrayoginī, and the ḍākinīs to powers the male figures cannot act without, a structural debt to Śākta theology the tantras do not conceal. In Purāṇic Hinduism, śakti became the umbrella for the great goddesses: Lakṣmī as Viṣṇu's energy, Pārvatī as Śiva's, Sarasvatī as Brahmā's — while the Devīmāhātmya and Devī Purāṇa went further, making the Devī the supreme power of which the gods are instruments. Medieval Europe met the idea through Jesuit accounts of the 'shaktis' of Śiva; modern yoga and global wellness vocabulary adopted the word wholesale, often stripped of the theology that insists she is not a mood but the motor of the divine.
lore.culturalLegacy: Śakti is the foundation of Śākta Hinduism, one of the four major devotional streams, centered on the Devī in her forms as Durgā, Kālī, Lalitā, and Tripurasundarī. Her festivals are among the largest on earth: Durgā-pūjā builds the goddess a whole temporary city each autumn, and Navarātri's nine nights re-enact the Devīmāhātmya battle. The Tantric lineages — Śrīvidyā still transmitted in initiations, the kuṇḍalinī vocabulary of haṭha-yoga — exported the concept globally: 'shakti' entered English as a loanword for spiritual energy in the nineteenth century through the Theosophists and through Vivekananda's Vedānta. Every yoga class that promises to 'raise your energy' is teaching Śakti's doctrine of the coiled serpent under another name.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Śakti is the answer to a question most traditions leave implicit: what does a god do? Not what he wills — what he does. The Hindu answer is that he acts through his śakti, and so the energy is not subordinate to the will but co-constitutive of it. This is why the Tantric maxim is so blunt: without her he is a corpse. Power, in this theology, is feminine not as a compliment but as an analysis.

To meditate on Śakti is to ask where your own power lives. The yogic tradition locates it coiled at the base of the spine, asleep, waiting for the discipline that will wake it — the striking image of capacity as something possessed long before it is known. Every capacity is like this: the ability to speak, to love, to endure existed in you before you exercised it. Śakti names the difference between what you are and what you can do — and makes the goddess of that difference.

lore.archaeology: Śakti's material record is the long history of goddess worship in South Asia. Kuṣāṇa-period Mathura (1st–3rd c. CE) yields early sculpted Devī and mother-goddess figures; Gupta and post-Gupta temples across Madhya Pradesh, Orissa, and Bengal install Durgā in her Mahiṣāsura-mardinī form, the Devīmāhātmya's battle rendered in stone. Copper and gold śrīcakra yantras, the Kālī images of Bengal, and the living pīṭhas — Kāmākhyā in Assam raised over the goddess's yoni, Kālīghāṭ in Kolkata — mark the tradition's sacred geography. The Devīmāhātmya itself survives in palm-leaf and paper manuscripts from the medieval period, the witnesses behind its modern critical edition.
